config.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array

intro.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function to find the smallest number in a rotated sorted array. You will learn how to apply binary search, a core algorithm for efficiently searching in sorted data, to solve this lesson. The main constructs involved are arrays, loops, and conditional logic in JavaScript. By the end, you'll understand how to adapt binary search for arrays that have been rotated, a common scenario in algorithm challenges.
intro.usecase: Finding the minimum in a rotated sorted array is a fundamental pattern used in systems that process time-series data or sorted datasets that may have been shifted. For example, in financial dashboards displaying stock prices over time, this algorithm helps identify the lowest price point after market hours when the data might be rotated. It's also essential in calendar applications that need to find the earliest available appointment slot in a rotated schedule, or in e-commerce filters that must locate the minimum price in a sorted product list that's been circularly shifted. Understanding this pattern enables developers to efficiently handle sorted data that arrives in non-standard orientations.

objectives: Implement a binary search algorithm to locate the minimum element in a rotated sorted array
Apply conditional logic to determine whether to search in the left or right half of the array
Initialize and manipulate pointers to track search boundaries during the algorithm execution
Construct a function that returns the minimum value when the search converges on a single element
Configure loop conditions to ensure the algorithm terminates correctly when the minimum is found
Update pointer positions based on comparisons between middle elements and array boundaries
Integrate edge case handling for arrays that are not rotated or contain duplicate values

content.body: Imagine you have a sorted list of numbers that's been rotated—like a circular shift. Your task is to find the smallest number in it. We'll learn how to do this efficiently using binary search, even when the array isn't perfectly sorted in the usual way.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
• Explain why binary search works on rotated sorted arrays.
• Implement an algorithm to find the minimum in a rotated sorted array.
• Identify which half of the array to discard at each step.
• Handle edge cases like already-sorted or single-element arrays.
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Look at this rotated sorted array: [5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3, 4]. Where is the smallest number? Is it in the left half (5-7) or the right half (1-4)? Think about how you'd decide.
content.title: Try it

content.body: Now consider [3, 4, 5, 1, 2]. If you check the middle element (5), what does it tell you about where the minimum could be? Can you eliminate half the array based on that?
content.title: Think deeper

content.body: You just used intuition to guess where the minimum might be. That's a good start, but we need a systematic way to always know which half to search next.
content.title: What you did

content.body: With a large rotated array, checking every element is too slow. We need a method that eliminates half the possibilities at each step. Can't figure it out? The next step will show you.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Binary search works here because even though the array is rotated, it's still made of two sorted halves. By comparing the middle element with the rightmost one, we can tell which half is properly sorted—and the minimum must be in the other half.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Repeatedly cut the range in half; only one half can contain the answer.

content.body: We'll use binary search but adapt it for rotation. Start with left and right pointers. At each step, compare the middle element with the rightmost element. If the middle is greater, the minimum is in the right half. If it's less, the minimum is in the left half (including middle). Keep cutting the search space in half until you find it.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Set left = 0, right = last index.
2. While left < right:
   a. Calculate mid index.
   b. If nums[mid] > nums[right], search right half (left = mid + 1).
   c. Else, search left half including mid (right = mid).
3. Return nums[left] (the minimum).
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up the function
steps.instruction: Create a function called findMin that takes an array nums as its parameter.
steps.hint: Use the function keyword or an arrow function.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the function is named findMin and takes nums as a parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's start with a basic function definition.

steps.title: Initialize pointers
steps.instruction: Inside the function, declare two variables: left starting at 0 and right starting at the last index of nums.
steps.hint: Use let for left and right. For right, use nums.length - 1.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've set up the search boundaries.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Check that left is 0 and right is nums.length - 1.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember to declare left and right with let.

steps.title: Implement the binary search loop
steps.instruction: Add a while loop that continues while left is less than right. Inside, calculate the mid index and compare nums[mid] with nums[right] to decide which half to search.
steps.hint: Use Math.floor((left + right) / 2) for mid. If nums[mid] > nums[right], move left to mid + 1. Otherwise, move right to mid.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! The loop correctly cuts the search space in half.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check your condition and the if-else logic. Remember to update left or right.
steps.feedbackWrong: Focus on the while loop and the comparison with nums[right].

steps.title: Return the result
steps.instruction: After the loop ends, return nums[left] (which will be the minimum element).
steps.hint: Add a return statement after the while loop.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure to return nums[left].
steps.feedbackWrong: Add a return statement after the loop.

content.body: You've implemented binary search for a rotated sorted array! Remember: the array must be sorted (even if rotated) for this to work. If the array isn't rotated, the algorithm still works—it'll just return the first element. Keep practicing with different rotations to solidify the 'cut in half' intuition.
